This activity focuses on building and using `LINESTRING` and `POLYGON` objects in `R`.  We will use them to ask an ecological question about dogwood trees sampled along a transect in Richmond, Virginia.

```{r}
#| message: false
library( sf )
library( tidyverse )
library( units )
```

You will also need the `terra` library installed (`install.packages("terra")`), though you will not load it yourself.  It is used inside the land cover function at the end.

## The Data

These are maternal dogwood trees from an ongoing study.  Each tree was sampled in one of two habitat types: `Cultivar` trees growing in suburban and urban Richmond and Chesterfield, and `Native` trees in Pocahontas State Park.  The columns are:

- `Type`: The habitat the tree was sampled in.
- `Tree`: An ID for the tree.
- `Longitude` and `Latitude`: Its location (decimal degrees, WGS84).
- `N`: The number of offspring (seeds) collected from that tree.

The data are in the course data repository at:

```{r}
url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_Dogwoods.csv"
```

## The Big Picture

The main question you are going to work on here is:

> Do the `Cultivar` and `Native` dogwoods live in different landscapes?  And does a single transect through the study area represent the landscape the trees actually live in?

To answer this, you will build lines and polygons around the trees and then measure the land cover inside them.  Keep the [`sf` cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/sf.pdf) handy.

## Land Cover

The land cover data are from the 2021 [National Land Cover Database](https://www.mrlc.gov/data) (NLCD), which classifies every 30 m × 30 m cell of the US into a land cover type.  These data are a *raster*, which we will learn to work with in a later topic.  For now, the function below does that part for you.  Run the chunk to load it, but you do not need to understand what is inside it yet.

To use it, pass `get_landcover()` an `sf` object of polygons.  It returns a `data.frame` with one row for each polygon and each of seven land cover categories (`Water`, `Developed`, `Barren`, `Forest`, `Shrub/Grass`, `Agriculture`, and `Wetland`).  The rows carry along all the columns from your polygons (but not the geometry) plus the `Proportion` of that polygon's area covered by that category.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The land cover function (run this, but don't worry about it yet)"
get_landcover <- function( polygons ) {
  nlcd_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_NLCD_2021.tif"
  nlcd_file <- file.path( tempdir(), "Richmond_NLCD_2021.tif" )
  if( !file.exists( nlcd_file ) || file.size( nlcd_file ) == 0 ) {
    download.file( nlcd_url, nlcd_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE )
  }
  nlcd <- terra::rast( nlcd_file )

  # Proportion of each polygon's area in each NLCD class
  areas <- terra::extract( nlcd,
                           terra::vect( sf::st_transform( polygons, terra::crs( nlcd ) ) ),
                           exact = TRUE )
  names( areas ) <- c("ID", "Code", "Fraction")

  # Group the 15 NLCD classes into 7 categories
  key <- tibble::tibble( Code = c(11, 21, 22, 23, 24, 31, 41, 42, 43, 52, 71, 81, 82, 90, 95),
                         Category = c("Water",
                                      "Developed", "Developed", "Developed", "Developed",
                                      "Barren",
                                      "Forest", "Forest", "Forest",
                                      "Shrub/Grass", "Shrub/Grass",
                                      "Agriculture", "Agriculture",
                                      "Wetland", "Wetland") )

  areas |>
    dplyr::inner_join( key, by = "Code" ) |>
    dplyr::mutate( Category = factor( Category, levels = unique( key$Category ) ) ) |>
    dplyr::group_by( ID, Category, .drop = FALSE ) |>
    dplyr::summarize( Cells = sum( Fraction ), .groups = "drop_last" ) |>
    dplyr::mutate( Proportion = Cells / sum( Cells ) ) |>
    dplyr::ungroup() |>
    dplyr::mutate( Category = as.character( Category ) ) |>
    dplyr::left_join( sf::st_drop_geometry( polygons ) |> dplyr::mutate( ID = dplyr::row_number() ),
                      by = "ID" ) |>
    dplyr::select( -ID, -Cells ) |>
    dplyr::relocate( Category, Proportion, .after = dplyr::last_col() )
}
```
